Fulfilling a customer's order › Stage 1: Place the order

Runbook: Place the order draft, generated from the register

An alert sent you here? Go to its entry.
Checkouts that ended with no orderHow many checkouts reaching Ordering API ended without their order being written?
New to this stage?
The stage on one page how a case moves through it, its outcomes, what is at stake

An online store selling outdoor clothing and equipment to signed-in customers through a web front end (and a mobile app), with orders accepted, stock-checked, paid and shipped by back-end services joined by a message broker. Configuration described: the Aspire AppHost as deployed to Azure Container Apps, with UseFoundry=true so the chat and embedding models are present; Postgres, RabbitMQ and Redis run as the application's own containers. proposed: no source says which configuration runs in production; this is the fullest the repository defines. In this configuration the services run outside Development, so /health is not mapped and logs default to Information.

StepRight outcomeFrom → toDone byNeeds
Expected outcome: The order is placed(proposed) an ordering.orders row in Submitted with one orderItems row per basket line at the catalogue price, the delivery address, and BuyerId and PaymentMethodId set(none) → SubmittedWebApp, ClientApp, Mobile BFF, Basket API, Catalog API, Ordering APIOrdering database, Basket store, Catalog database, Identity API
Step 1.1: The customer's basket is emptied(proposed) the buyer's basket is gone once the order exists(none) → (none)WebApp, ClientApp, Basket API, Ordering APIBasket store, Event bus

Expected of the stage. A case that enters it leaves within the promise (proposed: none assumed by the code beyond one request: placing is a single call (“The order is placed”), bounded only by the HTTP client's resilience defaults), in one of these ways:

  • Expected outcome: The order is placed: (proposed) an ordering.orders row in Submitted with one orderItems row per basket line at the catalogue price, the delivery address, and BuyerId and PaymentMethodId set

What is at stake.

  • Order id ("Id"): The only key that joins the order across services and to the customer
  • Order total (sum of Units x UnitPrice): Money the customer pays; value blocked while the order is stuck
  • Items and units (ordering."orderItems"): What must be in stock and shipped
  • Buyer (ordering.buyers "IdentityGuid"): Who is waiting and who is told
  • Delivery address: Where the goods must arrive
  • Payment method (card number masked to the last four digits): What is charged
  • Customer experience and trust, if “The order is placed” fails: counted in checkouts that emptied the basket and created no order. Ordering API answers 200 even when the order was not written, and the WebApp empties the basket without reading the answer
  • Customer experience and trust, if “The customer's basket is emptied” fails: counted in baskets still holding items already ordered. Both deletes failed; the customer may order the items twice
Reference, used by every entry
Every check, written once

Is Ordering database down or unreachable?

Used by Checkouts that ended with no orderPart Ordering databaseReads Checkouts that ended with no order; Ordering database accepting connections
How to check
In the postgres container (az containerapp exec --name postgres --resource-group <rg>) run pg_isready -d orderingdb
Not the cause if accepting connections
The cause if no response, or rejecting connections
‹ Back to Checkouts that ended with no order
Ending Yes → Restore: action 1
Why this check reads it this way
The ordering database does not answer: the transaction around the create command cannot begin and the request check runs outside the command's try, so Ordering API answers with an error and writes no 'CreateOrderCommand' result line; the WebApp does not read the answer and empties the basket

Is Ordering database slow?

Used by Checkouts that ended with no orderPart Ordering databaseReads Checkouts that ended with no order; Long-running statements on orderingdb
How to check

In the postgres container (az containerapp exec --name postgres --resource-group <rg>) run psql -U postgres -d orderingdb, then:

SELECT count(*) FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE datname = 'orderingdb' AND state = 'active' AND now() - query_start > interval '5 seconds';
Not the cause if 0
The cause if 1 or more, persisting
‹ Back to Checkouts that ended with no order
Ending Yes → Can’t restore here: escalate to the owner of Ordering database
Why this check reads it this way
Statements on the ordering database run long: the create command's transaction outlasts the WebApp's resilience handler, which retries with the same x-requestid, or fails and answers with an error

Is Ordering database full or out of capacity?

Used by Checkouts that ended with no orderPart Ordering databaseReads Checkouts that ended with no order; Connections to the postgres server against max_connections
How to check

In the postgres container (az containerapp exec --name postgres --resource-group <rg>) run psql -U postgres -d orderingdb, then:

SELECT count(*) FROM pg_stat_activity;
SHOW max_connections;
Not the cause if well below max_connections
The cause if at max_connections
‹ Back to Checkouts that ended with no order
Ending Yes → Restore: action 1
Why this check reads it this way
The shared postgres server refuses new connections: the create command fails as when the database does not answer, with an error and no order

Is the act failing inside Ordering API?

Used by Checkouts that ended with no orderPart Ordering APIReads Checkouts that ended with no order; Order requests answered OK with no order created
How to check
Search the console log of ordering-api (az containerapp logs show --name ordering-api --resource-group <rg> --type console --tail 300 --format text (one replica per call; add --replica for the others)) for 'CreateOrderCommand failed - RequestId:' and, just before each, 'Validation errors - CreateOrderCommand' (a refusal, with its errors), or 'Handling command CreateOrderCommand' with no 'Command CreateOrderCommand handled' line after it (the handler threw; Ordering.API/Application/Behaviors/LoggingBehavior.cs:9-11)
Not the cause if no 'CreateOrderCommand failed' line
The cause if the failed line, after a validation error or a handler that did not finish
‹ Back to Checkouts that ended with no order
Ending Yes → Can’t restore here: escalate to the owner of Ordering API
Why this check reads it this way
The order is not written: its validation refuses the command, or its handler throws, and the identified-command handler swallows either into false with nothing logged for it. Ordering API still answers 200 and logs 'CreateOrderCommand failed'

Is Ordering API answering with errors?

Used by Checkouts that ended with no orderPart Ordering APIReads Checkouts that ended with no order; Order requests answered OK with no order created; Ordering API requests by route and status, and their duration
How to check
Search the console log of ordering-api (az containerapp logs show --name ordering-api --resource-group <rg> --type console --tail 300 --format text (one replica per call; add --replica for the others)) for the 'Sending command:' lines of the create command, each naming its request id (Ordering.API/Apis/OrdersApi.cs:148-153), and for each request id the line 'CreateOrderCommand succeeded - RequestId:' or 'CreateOrderCommand failed - RequestId:' (:159, :163)
Not the cause if every request id has a succeeded line
The cause if a request id with a failed line, or with neither (the request threw)
‹ Back to Checkouts that ended with no order
Ending Yes → Can’t restore here: escalate to the owner of Ordering API
Why this check reads it this way
Ordering API answers a checkout without writing its order: with 200 after the command returned false, or with an error when the request threw before the command ran. The WebApp does not read the answer, empties the basket and shows the orders page, so the customer is not told. This test lists the checkouts; the tests before it say why
Causes the design rules out, so no check is needed
  • Ordering API, Catalog API and Basket API, callee down: as a cause of checkouts that reach Ordering API and end with no order (“Checkouts that ended with no order”). Where Catalog API, Basket API or Ordering API cannot be reached, the WebApp's call throws: the basket and item reads before the order call, and the order call's send itself. The exception leaves the checkout before the basket is deleted and before the orders page is shown, so the checkout fails in front of the customer with nothing written. Counted by the WebApp's errors, “WebApp rate, errors, duration”
  • Mobile BFF, callee down: as a cause of checkouts that reach Ordering API and end with no order (“Checkouts that ended with no order”). Where Mobile BFF cannot be reached, the mobile app's post fails at the app and nothing reaches Ordering API. Counted by “Mobile app order and cancel calls that fail”, the mobile app's failed order calls
  • Catalog API and Basket API, callee returns an error: as a cause of checkouts that reach Ordering API and end with no order (“Checkouts that ended with no order”). Basket API's gRPC error and Catalog API's error status both throw in the WebApp before the order call, so the checkout fails in front of the customer. Counted by “Basket API rate, errors, duration” and “Catalog API rate, errors and duration”
  • Ordering API, Catalog API and Basket API, callee slow or hangs: as a cause of checkouts that reach Ordering API and end with no order (“Checkouts that ended with no order”). A call that outlasts the standard resilience handler every HTTP client carries throws in the WebApp before the basket is deleted, so the customer sees the checkout fail; a retried order call carries the same x-requestid and writes at most one order. Counted by the callees' durations, “Ordering API requests by route and status, and their duration”, “Catalog API rate, errors and duration” and “Basket API rate, errors, duration”
  • WebApp and ClientApp, caller gives up mid-call: as a cause of checkouts that reach Ordering API and end with no order (“Checkouts that ended with no order”). A front end that gives up shows the customer a failed checkout and keeps the basket; an order already written stands, with its succeeded line. Counted by “WebApp rate, errors, duration” and “Mobile app order and cancel calls that fail”
  • Ordering API, Catalog API and Basket API, callee answers wrongly: as a cause of checkouts that reach Ordering API and end with no order (“Checkouts that ended with no order”). A wrong answer still writes an order. Basket API's lines and Catalog API's names and prices go into the order as answered: the expected outcome “The order is placed”'s wrong outcome, which no record counts (measure-gaps the expected outcome “The order is placed”). Ordering API's answer is not read
  • Ordering API, the act completes wrongly: as a cause of checkouts that reach Ordering API and end with no order (“Checkouts that ended with no order”). The order is written from the request as sent; a wrong line comes from the basket or catalogue answer, the expected outcome “The order is placed”'s wrong outcome, which no record counts (measure-gaps the expected outcome “The order is placed”)
  • Ordering database, answers stale or wrong: as a cause of checkouts that reach Ordering API and end with no order (“Checkouts that ended with no order”). Ordering API reads and writes one postgres server with no replica, and the order is built from the request, not from what the database holds
  • Basket store, unavailable: as a cause of checkouts that reach Ordering API and end with no order (“Checkouts that ended with no order”). For the Basket store: the basket read fails in Basket API and throws in the WebApp before the order call, so the checkout fails in front of the customer; at emptying, the basket is not deleted. Counted by “Basket store reachable and memory used” and “Basket API rate, errors, duration”. A basket left holding ordered items is step 1.1's wrong outcome, which no record counts (measure-gaps step 1.1)
  • Basket store, slow: as a cause of checkouts that reach Ordering API and end with no order (“Checkouts that ended with no order”). For the Basket store: the basket read and delete are late; one outlasting the resilience handler throws as when the store does not answer. Counted by “Basket store reachable and memory used” and “Basket API rate, errors, duration”. A basket left holding ordered items is step 1.1's wrong outcome, which no record counts (measure-gaps step 1.1)
  • Basket store, full or out of capacity: as a cause of checkouts that reach Ordering API and end with no order (“Checkouts that ended with no order”). For the Basket store: Redis refusing writes or connections fails the basket read or delete as when it does not answer. Counted by “Basket store reachable and memory used”. A basket left holding ordered items is step 1.1's wrong outcome, which no record counts (measure-gaps step 1.1)
  • Basket store, answers stale or wrong: as a cause of checkouts that reach Ordering API and end with no order (“Checkouts that ended with no order”). For the Basket store: a wrong basket becomes the order's lines: the expected outcome “The order is placed”'s wrong outcome, which no record counts (measure-gaps the expected outcome “The order is placed”). A basket left holding ordered items is step 1.1's wrong outcome, which no record counts (measure-gaps step 1.1)
  • Catalog database, unavailable: as a cause of checkouts that reach Ordering API and end with no order (“Checkouts that ended with no order”). For the Catalog database: Catalog API cannot read the items and its error throws in the WebApp before the order call, so the checkout fails in front of the customer. Counted by “Catalog database accepting connections” and “Catalog API rate, errors and duration”
  • Catalog database, slow: as a cause of checkouts that reach Ordering API and end with no order (“Checkouts that ended with no order”). For the Catalog database: the item lookup is late; one outlasting the resilience handler throws as above. Counted by “Long-running statements on catalogdb” and “Catalog API rate, errors and duration”
  • Catalog database, full or out of capacity: as a cause of checkouts that reach Ordering API and end with no order (“Checkouts that ended with no order”). For the Catalog database: the shared postgres server refusing Catalog API's connections fails the lookup as above. Counted by “Connections to the postgres server from catalogdb”
  • Catalog database, answers stale or wrong: as a cause of checkouts that reach Ordering API and end with no order (“Checkouts that ended with no order”). For the Catalog database: a wrong name or price is written into the order: the expected outcome “The order is placed”'s wrong outcome, which no record counts (measure-gaps the expected outcome “The order is placed”)
  • Identity API, unavailable: as a cause of checkouts that reach Ordering API and end with no order (“Checkouts that ended with no order”). For Identity API: Ordering API validates the customer's token with signing keys its JWT handler fetches from Identity API and keeps; without them the order call is refused at authentication and no command line is written, so “Checkouts that ended with no order” does not see it. The WebApp still empties the basket. Counted by “Ordering API requests by route and status, and their duration”, Ordering API's answers by route and status, and “Identity API rate, errors, duration”
  • Identity API, slow: as a cause of checkouts that reach Ordering API and end with no order (“Checkouts that ended with no order”). For Identity API: the key fetch is made by the JWT handler, not on every request: a slow Identity API delays only the requests that wait on it. Counted by “Identity API rate, errors, duration”
  • Identity API, full or out of capacity: as a cause of checkouts that reach Ordering API and end with no order (“Checkouts that ended with no order”). For Identity API: a refusal shows as when Identity API does not answer: the order call refused at authentication. Counted by “Ordering API requests by route and status, and their duration” and “Identity API rate, errors, duration”
  • Identity API, answers stale or wrong: as a cause of checkouts that reach Ordering API and end with no order (“Checkouts that ended with no order”). For Identity API: keys out of date make the order call refused at authentication, as when Identity API does not answer. Counted by “Ordering API requests by route and status, and their duration”
  • Basket API, callee down: as a cause of checkouts that end with no order (“Checkouts that ended with no order”): the order is already written when the basket is emptied, beside the order call. Basket API cannot be reached and the WebApp's delete throws after the order was sent. The basket keeps the ordered items: step 1.1's wrong outcome, which no record counts (measure-gaps step 1.1)
  • Basket API, callee returns an error: as a cause of checkouts that end with no order (“Checkouts that ended with no order”): the order is already written when the basket is emptied, beside the order call. Basket API answers the delete with an error. The basket keeps the ordered items: step 1.1's wrong outcome, which no record counts (measure-gaps step 1.1)
  • Basket API, callee slow or hangs: as a cause of checkouts that end with no order (“Checkouts that ended with no order”): the order is already written when the basket is emptied, beside the order call. the delete is late, or outlasts the resilience handler and throws. The basket keeps the ordered items: step 1.1's wrong outcome, which no record counts (measure-gaps step 1.1)
  • WebApp and ClientApp, caller gives up mid-call: as a cause of checkouts that end with no order (“Checkouts that ended with no order”): the order is already written when the basket is emptied, beside the order call. a front end that gives up leaves the delete to Basket API's own handler of the order-started event. The basket keeps the ordered items: step 1.1's wrong outcome, which no record counts (measure-gaps step 1.1)
  • Basket API, callee answers wrongly: as a cause of checkouts that end with no order (“Checkouts that ended with no order”): the order is already written when the basket is emptied, beside the order call. Basket API's answer to the delete carries nothing the front end acts on. The basket keeps the ordered items: step 1.1's wrong outcome, which no record counts (measure-gaps step 1.1)

The basket keeps the ordered items: step 1.1's wrong outcome, which no record counts (measure-gaps step 1.1)

The basket keeps the ordered items: step 1.1's wrong outcome, which no record counts (measure-gaps step 1.1)
  • Ordering API, relay not running: as a cause of checkouts that end with no order (“Checkouts that ended with no order”): the order is already written when the basket is emptied, beside the order call. there is no relay to stop: the request that committed the change publishes right after its commit. The basket keeps the ordered items: step 1.1's wrong outcome, which no record counts (measure-gaps step 1.1)

The basket keeps the ordered items: step 1.1's wrong outcome, which no record counts (measure-gaps step 1.1)

The basket keeps the ordered items: step 1.1's wrong outcome, which no record counts (measure-gaps step 1.1)

The basket keeps the ordered items: step 1.1's wrong outcome, which no record counts (measure-gaps step 1.1)

Restore one card per action; each returns you to your entry

After any action that restores: go back to the entry of the alert that fired and run its checks again for every case still affected, since a restore can leave cases in other states.

Action 1: restore

Needs approval before it is run.

Have the database owner bring the postgres server back to accepting connections, checking first where its data lives before any restart (what not to do; no data volume is declared). All four databases share it; then re-drive orders left in AwaitingValidation or StockConfirmed (restore action 2)

Expected pg_isready -d orderingdb, run in the postgres container, answers accepting connections, and order-processor stops logging 'Error querying confirmed grace period orders'
If different If pg_isready answers accepting connections and order-processor still logs the error, the fault is Order Processor's own connection: escalate to its owner
‹ Back to Checkouts that ended with no order: Is Ordering database down or unreachable? ‹ Back to Checkouts that ended with no order: Is Ordering database full or out of capacity?

Action 2: re-drive

Needs approval before it is run.

First clear the cause the test found (its part restored: the broker by restore action 3, the postgres server by restore action 1; or its owner engaged). Then list the orders still held once queues Ordering, Catalog and PaymentProcessor have drained (“Queue Ordering: messages waiting and consumers”, “Queue Catalog: messages waiting and consumers” and “Queue PaymentProcessor: messages waiting and consumers”): in the postgres container (az containerapp exec --name postgres --resource-group <rg>) run psql -U postgres -d orderingdb, then:

SELECT "Id", "OrderStatus" FROM ordering.orders WHERE "OrderStatus" IN ('AwaitingValidation','StockConfirmed') AND now() - "OrderDate" > interval '2 minutes';

Send them back to the start of the stage:

UPDATE ordering.orders SET "OrderStatus" = 'Submitted' WHERE "Id" IN (<ids>) AND "OrderStatus" IN ('AwaitingValidation','StockConfirmed');

Move the orders only by this reset to Submitted: do not set them on to a later status by hand (what not to do), resend their outbox rows (what not to do), look for their failed messages to replay (what not to do), or restart order-processor for them (what not to do).

Expected Within about 30 seconds Order Processor logs 'Publishing integration event:' for each id, the orders reach AwaitingValidation, and about 20 seconds later Paid or Cancelled; the count of orders held past the promise falls
If different Orders still in Submitted after a minute: work the Submitted branch. Otherwise escalate

Action 3: restore

Needs approval before it is run.

Have the broker's owner bring eventbus back, checking first where its data lives before any restart (what not to do; the AppHost declares no data volume); then restart each service whose log shows 'Error starting RabbitMQ connection' (restore action 4); then re-drive orders left in AwaitingValidation or StockConfirmed (restore action 2)

Expected rabbitmq-diagnostics -q ping, run in the eventbus container, succeeds and every queue has a consumer
If different Escalate
‹ Back to Action 4

Action 4: restore

Restart the service whose queue has no consumer or binding (ordering-api, catalog-api or payment-processor):

az containerapp revision restart --name <service> --resource-group <rg> --revision <its active revision, from az containerapp revision list>
Expected rabbitmqctl list_queues shows consumers 1 or more on its queue, list_bindings shows its routing keys, and waiting messages drain
If different If its log shows 'Error starting RabbitMQ connection' again, the broker is the cause: restore action 3

What not to do.

  • Do not restart the postgres or eventbus container apps as a first move: no data volume is declared for either, so find out where their data lives first
  • Do not set "OrderStatus" straight to 'StockConfirmed', 'Paid' or 'Cancelled' by SQL: the events are raised only inside the setters, so no outbox row is written and nothing after it happens (payment, stock reduction, notifications)
  • Do not set an outbox row's "State" back to 0 to have it sent: nothing reads unsent rows after the request that wrote them
  • Do not look for failed messages to replay: a consumer acknowledges a message it failed on, and no dead-letter queue exists
  • Do not restart order-processor to move orders held in AwaitingValidation or StockConfirmed: the poll selects only Submitted

Before you start: the access you need

You need to be able to read each of these. A check you cannot run is a gap in this runbook: note it.

  • Order: Checkouts that ended with no order; Order requests answered OK with no order created
  • Ordering API: Ordering API requests by route and status, and their duration
  • Ordering database: Ordering database accepting connections; Long-running statements on orderingdb; Connections to the postgres server against max_connections
  • Deployment, configuration and restart history for WebApp, ClientApp, Mobile BFF, Basket API, Catalog API, Ordering API, Identity API.

Runbook: Place the order › Alert

Checkouts that ended with no order

A checkout that reaches Ordering API and writes no order leaves the customer with no order and, on the web front end, an emptied basket and the orders page, so the customer is not told. A checkout that never reaches Ordering API fails in front of the customer and is not counted here; nor is an order call refused at authentication, which writes no command line (Ordering API's answers by status show it)

It has been above the operators’ threshold for longer than their window (the alert).

Its cases those that left by “The order is placed” from the case is created in the alert's window. A case still in the stage is not one of this alert's.
Look back from when the earliest of its cases entered the stage, to now: what sent a case out wrongly can come before it left.
Do now
  1. List its cases and set the look-back. Every check below runs on these cases, over that time. List them with the alert’s own count:
    How
    ordering-api log over the window, by request id: those with a 'Sending command:' line for the create command (Ordering.API/Apis/OrdersApi.cs:148-153) and no 'CreateOrderCommand succeeded - RequestId:' line (:159), that is the 'CreateOrderCommand failed - RequestId:' lines (:163) and the requests that threw before answering; against all such request ids. A retried call carries the same request id and counts once
  2. Contain. Hold each case the alert lists where it is now (Submitted): move none of them on until the failing part's owner has ruled. It left by the stage's main ending with a wrong outcome, and every later move carries that outcome on.
  3. Do not restart the postgres or eventbus container apps as a first move: no data volume is declared for either, so find out where their data lives first
  4. Do not set "OrderStatus" straight to 'StockConfirmed', 'Paid' or 'Cancelled' by SQL: the events are raised only inside the setters, so no outbox row is written and nothing after it happens (payment, stock reduction, notifications)
  5. Do not set an outbox row's "State" back to 0 to have it sent: nothing reads unsent rows after the request that wrote them
  6. Do not look for failed messages to replay: a consumer acknowledges a message it failed on, and no dead-letter queue exists
  7. Do not restart order-processor to move orders held in AwaitingValidation or StockConfirmed: the poll selects only Submitted
  8. Escalate or declare as soon as a trigger is met, at any point below. Triggers ›
Check first
1Is this already known?
How
Look for an open incident, or a known error with a fix in flight, for any of these parts: WebApp, ClientApp, Mobile BFF, Basket API, Catalog API, Ordering API, Ordering database, Basket store, Catalog database, Identity API, Event bus. Not the cause if there is none; the cause if one is open: link it and close.
Yes → Already known
2Was it planned?
How
Look for a maintenance window on any of those parts, or a planned change to a timing the stage depends on (WebApp's HTTP clients carry the standard resilience handler; a repeated POST with the same x-requestid is answered without a second order; No timeout of its own. The WebApp's basket delete is a gRPC call whose client is made by the HTTP client factory, so it carries the standard resilience handler: each attempt 10 seconds, up to 3 retries, 30 seconds in all. Basket API's delete on OrderStartedIntegrationEvent has no clock: the message waits in queue Basket until it is consumed, and the queue sets no expiry). Not the cause if there is none; the cause if a window is open or a setting was changed on purpose: link it and close.
Yes → Planned change
3Did something change when it started?
How
Look for any deploy, configuration change or unplanned restart of those parts since the look-back time above. Not the cause if there is none; the cause if a change lines up with the start.
Yes → Roll the change back, or escalate to the owner of the part that changed
4Is it already recovering?
How
Read the alert's own count over one window. Not the cause if it is not falling; a falling count means only that no new cases are arriving, and the cases it counted stay wrong: this check never closes the alert, so go on and work them.
Yes → No new cases: go on and work the ones it counted
Find the cause in order, on its cases only. No → next check. Yes → take its ending for the cases it lists, and go on for the rest. A check whose evidence lists no cases (a match in a log or a metric) explains no case by itself: note it, if the match falls inside the look-back, and go on; a case no later check explains takes the ending of every check noted for it, each named in the hand-over; where those endings differ, escalate rather than restore. A result you cannot read, or a check you cannot run: note it for the hand-over and go on. Where a command asks for a time span in angle brackets, give it the look-back above; where it asks for case ids in angle brackets, give it the ids of the cases you are working.
Is it up?
1Is Ordering database down or unreachable?
How
How to check
In the postgres container (az containerapp exec --name postgres --resource-group <rg>) run pg_isready -d orderingdb
Not the cause if accepting connections
The cause if no response, or rejecting connections
The same check in the reference ›
Yes → Restore: action 1
This alert's own causes
2Is Ordering database slow?
How
How to check

In the postgres container (az containerapp exec --name postgres --resource-group <rg>) run psql -U postgres -d orderingdb, then:

SELECT count(*) FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE datname = 'orderingdb' AND state = 'active' AND now() - query_start > interval '5 seconds';
Not the cause if 0
The cause if 1 or more, persisting
The same check in the reference ›
Yes → Can’t restore here: escalate to the owner of Ordering database
3Is Ordering database full or out of capacity?
How
How to check

In the postgres container (az containerapp exec --name postgres --resource-group <rg>) run psql -U postgres -d orderingdb, then:

SELECT count(*) FROM pg_stat_activity;
SHOW max_connections;
Not the cause if well below max_connections
The cause if at max_connections
The same check in the reference ›
Yes → Restore: action 1
4Is the act failing inside Ordering API?
How
How to check
Search the console log of ordering-api (az containerapp logs show --name ordering-api --resource-group <rg> --type console --tail 300 --format text (one replica per call; add --replica for the others)) for 'CreateOrderCommand failed - RequestId:' and, just before each, 'Validation errors - CreateOrderCommand' (a refusal, with its errors), or 'Handling command CreateOrderCommand' with no 'Command CreateOrderCommand handled' line after it (the handler threw; Ordering.API/Application/Behaviors/LoggingBehavior.cs:9-11)
Not the cause if no 'CreateOrderCommand failed' line
The cause if the failed line, after a validation error or a handler that did not finish
The same check in the reference ›
Yes → Can’t restore here: escalate to the owner of Ordering API
5Is Ordering API answering with errors?
How
How to check
Search the console log of ordering-api (az containerapp logs show --name ordering-api --resource-group <rg> --type console --tail 300 --format text (one replica per call; add --replica for the others)) for the 'Sending command:' lines of the create command, each naming its request id (Ordering.API/Apis/OrdersApi.cs:148-153), and for each request id the line 'CreateOrderCommand succeeded - RequestId:' or 'CreateOrderCommand failed - RequestId:' (:159, :163)
Not the cause if every request id has a succeeded line
The cause if a request id with a failed line, or with neither (the request threw)
The same check in the reference ›
Yes → Can’t restore here: escalate to the owner of Ordering API
None of these explains the cases left.Escalate with what you have
